title: Capillary self-folding chains
authors: Megan Delens, Axel Franckart, Martin Poty, Nicolas Vandewalle
abstract: Mesoscale self-assembly provides a route toward the design of programmable microsystems. Here, we construct flexible chains of floating monomers whose curved branches impose upward or downward deformations of the liquid interface, corresponding to effective positive or negative capillary charges. These geometrically encoded deformations generate local attractive or repulsive interactions along the chain. By tuning the capillary sequence, we obtain distinct folded configurations, including straight lines, zigzag patterns, and loops. For short chains, folding is largely governed by nearest-neighbor interactions and leads to well-defined structures. As the chain length increases and non-neighboring segments come into proximity and interact, however, the folding landscape becomes increasingly complex, with multiple metastable states whose number grows exponentially with chain length. We map these landscapes numerically and demonstrate experimentally that mechanical agitation allows the chains to transition between metastable configurations. Beyond encoding a target geometry, the capillary sequence therefore controls the complexity of the folding landscape as well as the degeneracy and mutational robustness of folded structures. These results establish capillary chains as a controllable mesoscale platform for investigating how local interaction rules give rise to collective folding and complex sequence-to-structure relationships reminiscent of those encountered in biomolecular systems.
summary: The authors demonstrate that flexible chains assembled at a liquid-air interface can self-fold based on local geometric interactions encoded by capillary charges. They show that while short chains fold predictably, longer chains possess an exponentially growing number of metastable folding states. This platform allows for the experimental and theoretical study of how simple local rules give rise to complex collective behavior, analogous to biomolecular folding.
main_problem: To investigate how a minimal, static, geometry-based interaction alphabet (capillary charges) can control not only the target conformation but also the complex metastable folding landscape of a connected chain.
main_result: The complexity and degeneracy of the folding landscape grow exponentially with chain length for long chains, and mechanical agitation is required to transition between these many metastable states.
method: Numerical mapping of energy landscapes derived from pair interaction potentials, complemented by experimental measurement using Schlieren profilometry and physical manipulation (agitation).
model_or_system: The system consists of flexible polymer chains made of floating monomers at a liquid-air interface. Interactions are governed by capillary charges ($Q$) encoded in the monomer geometry, leading to pair potentials derived from the modified Laplace equation.
key_observables: Number of metastable macrostates ($|G|$), energy landscape $U(s)$, Hamming distance ($d_H$), and the final folded ground state configuration.
important_parameters: Capillary length ($\lambda \approx 2.7$ mm for water-air interface); local interaction rules defined by capillary charges $\{+,+\}, \{-,-\}, \{-,+\}, \{+-\}$.
main_assumptions: The use of the Linear Superposition Approximation (LSA) to model the total interface deformation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate chain structures, measured/simulated liquid profiles for monomer assembly, energy landscapes for dimer cases, and scaling plots showing exponential growth of metastable states with chain length N.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the physical platform and interaction model using capillary charges. It then analyzes the folding behavior, demonstrating that while short chains are deterministic, longer chains exhibit exponentially growing complexity in their energy landscape. Finally, it explores how single-element mutations affect this complex folding landscape.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly controllable mesoscale platform where local rules (capillary charges) dictate emergent collective behavior (folding). The study of the exponential growth of metastable states and the role of external agitation mirrors concepts in glassy dynamics, energy minimization pathways, and frustrated systems relevant to statistical mechanics.

By using the reflection of a striped pattern, the local deformations of the liquid interface are evidenced. Negative and positive curvatures are visible near branch tips. Scale bar: 10 mm.

FIG. 4. Experimental liquid profiles around self-folding chains in same color scale as Figure 2 (red: positive, blue: negative surface deformations). Three N = 8 examples. (A) Linear structure obtained with a straight-biased code. (B) Zigzag when pairs of successive tips attract. (C) Loop formed with a fold-biased code.

FIG. 3. (A) The 16 possible capillary codes for a dimer, color-coded by stable state s ∈{−1, 0, +1}. Symmetric and asymmetric bistable codes are distinguished (full green and dashed green outlines). (B) Normalized capillary energy land- scapes U(s) computed from Eq. (5) using experimental pa- rameters (Qc = −0.075|Qb|). (C) Same landscapes computed with an enhanced central charge (Qc = −10|Qb|) to highlight symmetry-breaking in the asymmetric bistable cases. Grey areas indicate forbidden regions due to steric contact.

FIG. 7. Experimental exploration of the folding landscape for a fold-biased chain with N = 10 under vertical vibration. (A- F) Selected snapshots from Supplementary Movie S2 showing distinct metastable configurations. Configuration (F) corre- sponds to a low-energy experimental macrostate, consistent with theoretical predictions.
